Am I to be car-ri-ed to the skies on comfortable beds of flowers,

While others struggle for the prize and sail through seas of blood?

People considered him a wonderful reader. At church gatherings he was always asked to read poetry. When he finished, the ladies would raise their hands and drop them helplessly into their laps, roll their eyes, and shake their heads, as if to say, “Words cannot describe it; it is too beautiful, TOO beautiful for this earthly world.”

Once the hymn was over, the Reverend Mr. Sprague became a human noticeboard. He read announcements about meetings, societies, and other matters until the list seemed likely to last until Judgment Day. This is a strange custom that Americans still maintain, even in cities, in this age when newspapers are everywhere. Often, the less reason there is for keeping an old custom, the harder it is to abolish it.

Then the minister began to pray. It was a fine, generous prayer, full of detail. He pleaded for the church and its little children; for the village’s other churches; for the village itself; for the county and the state; for state officials; for the United States and all its churches; for Congress, the President, and government officials; for poor sailors thrown about on stormy seas; for the oppressed millions suffering beneath European kings and Eastern tyrants; for people who have the light and the good news but cannot see or hear them; and for unbelievers on distant islands. He ended by asking that the words he was about to speak might be received with grace and favor, like seeds planted in rich soil that would eventually produce a welcome harvest of goodness. Amen.

Dresses rustled as the standing congregation sat down. The boy whose story this book tells had not enjoyed the prayer. He had merely put up with it—if he had even managed that. He had fidgeted throughout, keeping an unconscious count of the prayer’s details. He was not listening, but he knew the familiar territory and the minister’s usual path through it. Whenever some small new item was slipped in, his ears caught it and his entire being rebelled. He thought additions were unfair and downright villainous. During the prayer a fly had landed on the back of the pew ahead of him. It tormented him by calmly rubbing its hands together, wrapping its arms around its head, and polishing the head so energetically that it seemed about to come off, revealing its thin thread of a neck. Then it scraped its wings with its back legs and smoothed them against its body as though they were the tails of a coat. It carried out its whole cleaning routine as peacefully as if it knew it was perfectly safe.

Mr. Bennet said almost nothing during dinner. Once the servants had left, however, he decided it was time to talk to his guest. He chose a subject on which he expected the man to excel, remarking that he seemed very fortunate in his patroness. Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s attention to his wishes and concern for his comfort seemed quite remarkable. Mr. Bennet could hardly have made a better choice. Mr. Collins praised her eloquently. The topic gave his manner an even greater solemnity than usual, and with an air of immense importance he declared that he had never encountered such behavior in anyone of high rank—such friendliness and willingness to notice an inferior as Lady Catherine had shown him. She had graciously approved both sermons he had already had the honor of delivering in her presence. She had also invited him to dine at Rosings twice and, only the previous Saturday, had sent for him to complete her evening game of quadrille. He knew that many people thought Lady Catherine proud, but he had found her invariably friendly. She always spoke to him as she would to any other gentleman. She had no objection whatsoever to his mixing with the neighborhood’s society or occasionally leaving his parish for a week or two to visit relatives. She had even been kind enough to advise him to marry as soon as possible, provided he chose wisely. Once she had visited his modest parsonage, thoroughly approved every improvement he had made, and even favored him with suggestions of her own: some shelves in the upstairs closets.

“That is all very proper and polite, I’m sure,” said Mrs. Bennet, “and I expect she is a very pleasant woman. It is a pity more great ladies aren’t like her. Does she live near you, sir?”

“Only a lane separates the garden containing my humble home from Rosings Park, her Ladyship’s residence.”

“I believe you said she was a widow, sir? Does she have any family?”

“She has just one daughter, the heiress to Rosings and a very considerable amount of property.”

“Ah,” exclaimed Mrs. Bennet, shaking her head, “then she is better provided for than many girls. And what kind of young lady is she? Is she beautiful?”

“She is an exceptionally charming young lady. Lady Catherine herself says that in true beauty Miss de Bourgh far surpasses the most beautiful women, because something in her features unmistakably identifies a young woman of distinguished birth.

Mr. Merton was deeply troubled by the second postponement of the wedding, and Lady Julia, who had already ordered her wedding outfit, did everything she could to persuade Sybil to end the engagement. But however dearly Sybil loved her mother, she had entrusted her whole life to Lord Arthur, and nothing Lady Julia said could shake her faith in him. Lord Arthur himself needed several days to recover from his terrible disappointment, and for a while his nerves were entirely shattered. His excellent common sense soon reasserted itself, however, and his sensible, practical mind did not leave him uncertain for long about his next step. Since poison had failed completely, dynamite, or another kind of explosive, was clearly the appropriate thing to try.

He therefore reviewed the list of his friends and relatives again and, after careful thought, decided to blow up his uncle, the Dean of Chichester. The Dean was a highly cultured and learned man with a great enthusiasm for clocks. He owned a remarkable collection of timepieces dating from the fifteenth century to the present, and Lord Arthur thought the good Dean’s hobby gave him a splendid opportunity to put his plan into practice. Where to obtain an explosive device was, of course, another question altogether. The London Directory offered no information on the subject. He also thought there would be little point in approaching Scotland Yard, since they never seemed to know anything about the activities of the dynamite faction until an explosion had already occurred, and even afterward knew very little.

Then he suddenly remembered his friend Rouvaloff, a young Russian with decidedly revolutionary inclinations, whom he had met at Lady Windermere’s during the winter. Count Rouvaloff was said to be writing a biography of Peter the Great. Supposedly he had come to England to study documents concerning that Tsar’s stay in the country as a ship’s carpenter. Most people suspected, however, that he was a Nihilist agent, and the Russian Embassy certainly regarded his presence in London with disapproval. Lord Arthur felt that this was precisely the man he needed. One morning he drove to the Count’s rooms in Bloomsbury to seek his advice and help.

‘So you are becoming seriously involved in politics?’ Count Rouvaloff asked, once Lord Arthur had explained the purpose of his visit. But Lord Arthur disliked any kind of boasting and felt obliged to confess that social questions did not interest him in the slightest. He simply wanted the explosive device for an entirely private family matter that concerned nobody but himself.
